title: Jungle sound, wa-wa and plunger trumpeters in Harlem
summary: He explains the wow-wow style of Johnny Dunn, Bubber Miley and Tommy Morris, and says Ellington built on it and that funk was not a music term.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Well, I wasn't trying for a sound, I was trying to eat, as I said before. You see, so it worked out. And from then on, now we're starting to have, people are starting to come in and wouldn't do very little dancing. We had to resort to such things like the blues and some of the little pop numbers in order to get them to dance. Because they were so sitting listening (unintelligible), and I had tried something new. I had tried using augmented chords, which gave it a sort of foreign effect. And at that time in wa-wa Harlem was stuck on jungle music and the wow-wow with Johnny Dunn, Tommy Morris, Bubba Miley, and Charley Evers, and Bobby Martin. Well, Bobby Martin eventually went with me, but that was the -- the wow-wow, they was using plungers and derbys and things like that, and it was more like a jungle. And that's

the one thing quiet as it's kept. That's the one thing that made Duke Ellington. The wa-wa and the plunger thing which he took from Bubber Miley, and he made a classic out of it. He using it with the whole band, but it really started - turned it into something by (unintelligible) Johnny Dunn was the first one. This Johnny Dunn, later on, worked with Mamie Smith and I guess Bessie Smith and Clara Smith and everybody else. But Johnny Dunn, he ended up with Lew Leslie, playing for Florence Mills, you see?

Yeah. See, so, but Johnny, Johnny, had it a little different from the others, because he was more so- wa-wa-ooed sophisticated wow-wow. In other words, he wow-wowed with-double.* But Tommy Morris and Bubber Miley, it was lowdown. What we called then the gutbucket, you see?
That was another term then, but in those days it wasn't used like it is today. Nobody spoke of funk, funky music. We spoke of funkiness for somebody that wouldn't take a bath.
So we didn't speak of funk in reference to music. That was a term that started way later since the Second World War. And I think they took that from Europe. Like the
Funk Studios in Germany and all like that, like (unintelligible), and stuff like that. But if you was to call somebody funky in those days, why you insulted them.
